title: You ran reset --hard and lost two commits. Get them back.
summary: Destroy a day of work with one command, then recover all of it. The reflog is the single most valuable thing a git user can know about.
mental_model: Commits are almost never deleted. `reset` only moves a branch pointer; the commits it moved away from are still in the object store, and the reflog wrote down where the pointer used to be. Recovery is just pointing the branch back.
danger: `reset --hard` also throws away uncommitted working-tree changes, and those are NOT in the reflog. Committed work is recoverable; unsaved edits are not.

write.content:
def clean(water):
    water.remove_debris()
    water.uv_sterilise()
    return water

steps.title: Note what you are about to lose
steps.why: Three commits. Write down that top subject line — in a moment it will vanish from `git log` entirely and you will need to recognise it when it reappears.

steps.title: The three resets, explained by doing the safe one
steps.why: `--soft` moves the branch pointer and keeps everything staged. Nothing is lost; the changes from the undone commit are sitting in your index, ready to be recommitted differently. This is the reset you actually want most of the time.
steps.expect: The UV change is now staged, not committed.

steps.title: Put it back
steps.why: Recommitting restores the state. Notice the sha changed — a commit is defined by its content AND its parent AND its message, so a recommit is a different object even with identical content.

steps.title: Now do the damage
steps.why: `--hard` moves the pointer and forcibly rewrites the working tree to match. Two commits just disappeared from history and the file on disk reverted. This is the moment people panic.
steps.expect: Only one commit left, and filter.py lost its debris and UV lines.

steps.title: Look at the reflog — the thing that saves you
steps.why: The reflog is a local journal of every position HEAD has held, kept for 90 days by default. It is not history; it is a record of pointer movements. Your 'lost' commits are right there, listed with the sha you need.
steps.expect: Entries reading 'reset: moving to HEAD~2', and above them your commits.

steps.title: Point the branch back and reclaim everything
steps.why: `HEAD@{1}` means 'wherever HEAD was one move ago'. Resetting hard onto it moves the branch back to the pre-disaster commit. All three commits return, files and all. Nothing was ever actually deleted.

verify.label: the lost commits are back
verify.hint: find the pre-reset sha in git reflog, then git reset --hard <sha>

steps.title: The other escape hatch
steps.why: Git also writes ORIG_HEAD before dangerous operations (reset, merge, rebase). `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` undoes the last one without you having to read the reflog at all.

verify.label: all three commits are back on main
verify.hint: git reflog, find the sha before the reset, then git reset --hard <sha>

verify.label: both lost commits recovered by subject
the working tree content came back too

pitfalls: The reflog is per-clone and never pushed. A fresh clone has no reflog — recovery must happen on the machine where the mistake was made.
`git reset --hard` with uncommitted changes is genuinely destructive. `git stash` first if you are unsure.
`git reset` moves a branch; `git revert` adds a new commit that undoes an old one. On a shared branch, revert is the honest choice.
`git fsck --lost-found` finds dangling commits even when the reflog has been pruned.
cheatsheet: move the branch, keep everything staged
move the branch, keep the files, unstage (the default)
